ai.definition: Neural telepathy devices are neurotechnological tools designed to facilitate direct brain-to-brain communication by decoding neural signals and transmitting them to another individual's brain.
ai.howItWorks: These devices work by capturing neural signals from the sender using sensors, processing these signals in real-time, and then transmitting them through a wireless connection to be decoded and interpreted by the recipient’s brain. This process enables seamless, non-verbal communication between individuals.
ai.problemSolved: They address the limitations of traditional methods of communication such as speech or writing, particularly for those with severe speech impairments or in situations where verbal communication is impractical or impossible.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves developing advanced sensor technology to accurately capture neural signals, sophisticated signal processing algorithms for real-time decoding and transmission, and miniaturized wireless transceivers for efficient data transfer.
ai.buildProcess: The build process begins with the design of biocompatible sensors that can be safely implanted or worn on the scalp. These sensors are then integrated with high-speed data processors and wireless communication modules to create a functional device capable of real-time neural signal processing and transmission.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include the development of advanced sensor technology, miniaturization of components for wearable devices, and the complexity of real-time signal processing algorithms. Additionally, regulatory compliance and clinical trials will significantly impact overall costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook suggests a long-term potential for commercialization but is currently in an early research phase with significant technical challenges and ethical considerations to address.
ai.regulation: Regulatory approval processes are complex due to the invasive nature of some devices and the need for rigorous safety and efficacy testing. Current regulatory frameworks may not fully cover these emerging technologies, necessitating new guidelines or standards.
ai.risks: Technical risks include signal interference, device failure, and potential long-term health effects from prolonged use. Ethical concerns revolve around privacy, consent, and the potential for abuse of such technology.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain at this stage due to high R&D costs, regulatory hurdles, and the need for extensive clinical validation. However, if successful, these devices could open up new markets in therapeutic applications and direct communication technologies.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving sensor accuracy, increasing transmission speeds, enhancing user interface design, and addressing ethical and safety concerns to ensure safe and effective deployment of neural telepathy devices.

glossary.def: The use of technology to interact with the nervous system, often involving the development and application of devices that can interface with or monitor brain activity.
Materials that are safe for use in contact with biological tissues without causing adverse effects, typically used in medical implants and devices.

subsystems.name: Neural recording front end
subsystems.role: picks up the electrical activity that carries a person's intention.
parts: endovascular electrodes placed via a blood vessel

subsystems.name: Decoder
subsystems.role: turns raw spikes and field potentials into something meaningful — intended movement, or phonemes and words.

subsystems.name: Transmission link
subsystems.role: carries the decoded signal from one person's system to another's.
parts: encoding into a compact signal another brain can accept

subsystems.name: Stimulation stage
subsystems.role: writes information into the receiving brain.
parts: implanted electrodes for direct cortical stimulation

subsystems.name: Closed-loop control
subsystems.role: keeps the pair synchronised as signals drift.

subsystems.name: Biostability and safety system
subsystems.role: keeps electrodes working and the user well over months and years.

buildSteps.title: Record neural activity
buildSteps.detail: Electrodes sit on or in the cortex (or on the scalp) and pick up voltage changes from thousands of neurons, which are amplified and digitised.

buildSteps.title: Stabilise and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Signals drift as tissue settles and electrodes move, so the system is retrained against known tasks — for example, asking the user to try to move a hand or speak a known sentence.

buildSteps.title: Decode intention
buildSteps.detail: Machine-learning models map activity patterns to intended movement direction or to phonemes and words; modern systems can decode attempted speech in paralysed people.

buildSteps.title: Compress to a transmissible signal
buildSteps.detail: Sending raw neural data is impractical, so the output is reduced to a small set of commands, tokens or a synthesised voice.

buildSteps.title: Deliver it to another brain
buildSteps.detail: The receiving side is stimulated — magnetic pulses or ultrasound through the skull, or implanted electrodes — producing a faint sensation, twitch or phosphene rather than a fully formed idea.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: Both users get feedback and the system continually recalibrates, because a stimulus that worked yesterday may not fire the same neurons today.

buildSteps.title: Prove it is safe and durable
buildSteps.detail: Any implanted version must survive years in tissue, stay hermetic and be removable or switchable off.

buildSteps.title: Scale bandwidth and meaning
buildSteps.detail: Only after recording and stimulation both get far finer could anything like fluent idea transfer be attempted — current links carry a handful of bits per minute.

prerequisites.why: arrays implanted in people work for months to a few years, and signal quality degrades as scar tissue forms.
speech and cursor control have been restored in small numbers of paralysed patients, but decoding general meaning is unsolved.
transcranial magnetic stimulation reaches only broad patches of cortex, far too coarse to write detailed information into a brain.

prerequisites.tech: Understanding of the neural code for concepts
prerequisites.why: we can map movements and words, but not abstract thought, so there is no signal to transmit.
wireless, sealed implants exist in neurostimulation devices, but not at the channel counts and lifetimes brain-to-brain links would need.

pathway.milestone: implanted and endovascular brain-computer interfaces restore typing or synthesised speech to a small number of severely paralysed people
pathway.unlocks: real clinical benefit from decoding, even with no transmission between people.

pathway.milestone: larger, more stable electrode arrays with faster wireless data and lower surgical risk
pathway.unlocks: longer-term use outside a few specialist centres.

pathway.milestone: laboratory two-person links carrying simple cues, building on experiments that pass motor or sensory signals between people using scalp recording and brain stimulation
pathway.unlocks: evidence about how much information a receiving brain can actually absorb.

pathway.milestone: shared semantic decoding between two people
pathway.unlocks: theoretical direct idea transfer, but only if the neural code for meaning is cracked — a research question, not an engineering schedule.
